title: Jürgen Habermas: Influential champion of modern democracy
subtitle: Remembering the philosopher of the public sphere
author: Rainer Forst
introduction: With the passing of philosopher Jürgen Habermas, we explore the enduring importance of his work on democracy, human rights, and the public sphere. Rainer Forst, Claudio Corradetti, and John S. Dryzek give their thoughts on Habermas and the legacy of his philosophical contributions - including his theory of communicative rationality, which laid bare both the power of ideas and the challenge of applying them in a complex and imperfect world.
body:
The Public Use of Reason: On the Death of Jürgen Habermas

With the passing of Jürgen Habermas, who shaped the humanities and social sciences of our time as perhaps no other thinker has, we lose a unique and irreplaceable intellectual voice. I have lost a teacher and interlocutor to whom I owe more than I can express.

To take the measure of his work, we must look back to the great figures of philosophy. The most natural comparison is with Immanuel Kant, for Habermas remained committed throughout his life to the Kantian imperative of illuminating our conditions of existence through the “public use of reason” — that is, through discourse among those affected. This theme runs through all his writings, which forge a new connection between philosophy and the social sciences: emancipation through communicative reason, a form of reason that seeks to recognise and overcome its own socially produced constraints. Drawing on Hegel, Marx, Weber, and Critical Theory, he radicalised the Kantian project.

No one matched Habermas in bringing together theoretical critique and political practice, binding the critique of ideology to standards of reason. This demanded an unerring sense for the most pressing problems of the day, both intellectual and social, and it never allowed him to rest. I witnessed this first-hand in the mid-1980s, when I studied with him as he simultaneously challenged post-structuralist philosophy and helped ignite the so-called Historikerstreit. In the former, his aim was to defend critical rationality; in the latter, to resist a regression in Germany’s historical consciousness.

These remained his central concerns to the very end: a sometimes desperate, but never hopeless, effort to think through radical democracy in its fullest sense and to work toward its realisation. In this respect, his work remains unfinished, even as it stands as a monument. He will be greatly missed — as a thinker of extraordinary breadth, a passionate intellectual, and a remarkable human being.

Rainer Forst is Professor of Political Theory and Philosophy at the Goethe University Frankfurt am Main.

A Farewell to Jürgen Habermas

When Europe emerged from the devastation of war, little remained of its democratic ideals. Even where fascism was not openly endorsed, the continent was shaped by authoritarian and illiberal cultures. A new democratic grammar had yet to be learned. Jürgen Habermas devoted his life and work to supporting this cultural and political transformation. He developed a philosophical model in which communication depends on pragmatic-transcendental conditions — sincerity, truthfulness, and normative validity — that make coordinated action possible. At the same time, he defended a procedural conception of democracy, in which the formation of political will begins with dispersed, informal processes of opinion-formation before moving into institutional channels.

SUGGESTED READING The paradox of democracy By Zac Gershberg

For generations of scholars, Habermas restored the hope of a renewed civic life. His idea of the co-originality of democracy and human rights enabled him to rethink, in post-metaphysical terms, the grounding of human rights. Even in the wake of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, such rights had often remained tied to Jacques Maritain’s notion of personalism — a largely Christian, Thomistic doctrine emphasising the primacy of the individual over the state. If Europe recovered from the collapse of reason, this was due in no small part to Habermas’s intellectual contribution.

Yet his thought was not without its blind spots. His later political interventions were marked by positions that many found obscure and difficult to justify, and which appeared to sit uneasily with his own philosophical commitments. For instance, his endorsement of the statement “Principles of Solidarity,” which expressed support for Israel and described its response as a “principally justified counter-strike,” published on 13 November 2023 on the website of Normative Orders, struck some as in tension with the universalist aspirations of his earlier work.

Claudio Corradetti is Professor of Political Philosophy at the University of Rome Tor Vergata.

Habermas and Deliberative Democracy

Deliberative democracy has been the dominant approach to democratic theory in the last two or three decades, increasingly too in practical democratic innovations. The basic idea is that democratic legitimacy rests on the right, opportunity, and capability of those subject to collective decisions (or their representatives) to participate in consequential deliberation about the decisions in question. This is a communication-centric view of democracy. The theory (though not the practical innovation) owes plenty to Jürgen Habermas. While deliberative democratic theory has many philosophical roots – including Aristotle, Burke, Mill, Dewey, Arendt – Habermas’s communication-centric philosophy (developed at length in The Theory of Communicative Action) became a key touchstone.

As history with practical intent, Habermas’s approach to democracy first appears in his 1962 German book, finally published in 1989 in English as Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere. This book established the crucial role in the development of democracy of a realm of free political communication among the early bourgeoisie confronting monarchy, aristocracy, and theocracy in Europe. Much later (in the 2000s), this dynamic interaction between public sphere and state would be echoed in the deliberative field’s turn to thinking about deliberative systems stretching from informal conversations in everyday life to authoritative collective decision, as opposed to deliberative forums. However, real-world deliberative innovations (such as citizens’ assemblies) have always followed the forum model.

Habermas’s communicative philosophy that had once grounded critical challenge to dominant institutions now justified those same institutions.

As normative political philosophy, Habermas’s own explicit model of democracy did not arrive until 1992 in German, published in English in 1996 as Between Facts and Norms. By then, others had already developed normative democratic theory strongly influenced by his ideas about critical theory and communicative action (including my own 1990 book, Discursive Democracy). Between Facts and Norms was massively influential, yet controversial because Habermas’s communicative philosophy that had once grounded critical challenge to dominant institutions now justified those same institutions – presenting an idealized picture of a liberal democratic state with deliberation in its public sphere protected by a familiar set of liberal rights, feeding into deliberation in parliament. This turn was welcomed by some in what James Bohman in 1998 called “the coming of age of deliberative democracy”, but seen by others as abandonment of the very idea of an emancipatory critical theory that so animated Habermas’s earlier work.

Today, the accommodationist view of the sort that appears in Between Facts and Norms is in the ascendant, particularly inasmuch as the key democratic task in many countries became the defence of existing institutions and practices against the rise of authoritarian populism, rather than pursuit of more authentic democracy. As deliberative democracy travels, the need for its grounding in relevant culturally-specific communicative practices has to move beyond Habermas’s Eurocentrism – though even that move can recognize Habermas’s own 1962 grounding of democratic possibilities in a particular culture and history. In all the debates in the deliberative field today, Habermas remains a key reference point. Like him or loathe him, he cannot be ignored.

John S. Dryzek is Distinguished Professor of Political Science at the University of Canberra.
